html:
The Chaco War was fought from 1932 to 1935 between Bolivia and Paraguay over the northern Gran Chaco, a hot, dry plain of thorn forest between the two countries. It was the bloodiest war in South America in the 1900s.

Bolivia had lost its coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific and wanted a way out to the Atlantic by the Paraguay River. Many on both sides also believed there was oil under the Chaco. Bolivia had more people and a bigger army, but its highland soldiers suffered badly in the heat and thirst of the lowlands, far from supplies. Paraguay fought close to home and won most of the battles. Tens of thousands of soldiers died, many of thirst and disease.

A truce came in 1935, and a treaty in 1938 gave Paraguay most of the land in dispute. Little oil was ever found there.

The war was fought across the lands of Chaco peoples such as the Nivaclé, Ayoreo, Enlhet and Maká. Some served as guides and scouts, and many lost land or were pushed from their homes. In Bolivia defeat discredited the old ruling class and fed the movements that made the revolution of 1952.
